        First, I explain compliance using a balloon as an example. Once we understand compliance,
    we apply that knowledge to the respiratory system. Before beginning, two points must be
       clear. One is that expanding the balloon requires a transmural pressure difference. What
     does transmural pressure difference mean? Mural refers to one side; transmural means
      across both sides of a single boundary.

          If you open a door, for instance, you push it outward. As you push, pressure on this side
     becomes greater than outside, so it moves outward. Another method is pulling from outside
      inward. In that case, you reduce external pressure so internal pressure remains the same,
     and it opens.





                                                                                                      1

In any case, whether you push here or pull outside, you create a pressure difference on this
wall of the door. That pressure difference moves the door, which is called transmural
pressure difference.

No movement occurs without creating a transmural pressure difference. This is also true for
the balloon. If you want to inflate it and bring more volume into it, you must create an
inside pressure greater than outside pressure. A transmural pressure difference pushes the
balloon’s wall outward, like opening the door, and air can pass through. Each step of
inflation requires producing a transmural pressure difference.

Transmural pressure difference is defined as inside pressure minus outside pressure. That
is one point to remember. The other point is that normally, what is the pressure in air? You
learned in the first lecture that we have air pressure here, which was 760 millimetres of
mercury. That is also one atmospheric pressure. Now, if I want to open this door, the
pressure inside is 760, outside is 760. If I push here, inside becomes 765, for example.
Outside is 760, so the pressure difference is 5. 765 minus 760. That drives the door open.
We always observe 760, then 765, and so on. In physiology, we simplify by setting external
air pressure to zero. Why do we do this? It does not reflect reality.

That is our practice: we treat the 760 pressure as zero, so both inside and outside the door
become zero. If you push the door, you create a pressure of 5 inside and zero outside,
which is easier for everyone to grasp than keeping 760 as the baseline.

This approach is familiar. When a physician measures your blood pressure and reports 100,
he is technically misleading you. If your blood pressure were truly 100, you would already
be dead; your actual pressure is 100 plus 760, or 860 millimetres of mercury. Your real
pressure is 860 millimetres of mercury, but if a physician said 860, you might think him
crazy and change doctors. He uses 100 because he sets 760 to zero, which is common in
medicine—except in one situation.

We must never do this when calculating partial pressures of gases, such as oxygen,
nitrogen, or carbon dioxide. If we set their pressure to zero because oxygen is part of the
air, oxygen pressure would also be zero, leaving no pressure. In those cases, we must
include the 760 air pressure and avoid setting it to zero; only with partial pressures are we
forbidden from doing so.
